name: Colin Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union, party or government. Nothing you say will be linked to your name, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It's a juggle. I feed the sheep and the handful of pigs first, then check the potatoes and the strawberry tunnels, and by nine I'm unlocking the farm shop at Elm Green Farm. My wife Anjali runs the shop and the little café most days, and my mum still does the scones on Saturdays. I love it when a family comes in and the kids see the piglets, and I'm worn out by trying to be a farmer and a shopkeeper at the same time.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mostly people from the new estate on the edge of town, commuters who work in offices in the city. They come at weekends for eggs, our sausages and a coffee. There's a regular, Mrs Hale, who's come every Saturday for eleven years and buys exactly one dozen eggs and one loaf, never more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's handy and leave it there. I use one of those chat programs now and then to write the shop's posts online, when Anjali's too busy, and it does a decent job if you tell it about the strawberries. I'd say to the regulars it's nothing to lose sleep over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For us it's no change, really. The shop lives or dies on weather and people's weekends. If nothing changes in hiring and pay, my customers keep coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as planned. We were going to put in a second coffee machine for summer, about three thousand, and finally fix the car park drainage. Maybe I'd use the chat program a bit more for the shop newsletter, once Anjali's cousin shows me properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pleased, if anything. One less thing to think about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has the chat program ever got something wrong for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once it wrote that our strawberries were organic, and they're not, we spray them twice a season. I caught it, but if a customer had read that, I'd have been in trouble with the trading people. So I read every word now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Mrs Hale think of AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say, as long as the eggs are still here, Colin. She doesn't have a smartphone. She pays in coins, counted out on the counter.

S0.say: It's handy and nothing to lose sleep over. I use a chat program now and then to write the shop's posts when Anjali's too busy.
S0.think: It's no real change for us, because the shop lives or dies on weather and people's weekends. If hiring and pay carry on, my customers keep coming.
S0.do: Buys the second coffee machine for summer for about three thousand and fixes the car park drainage, as planned. Uses the chat program a bit more for the newsletter once a relative shows him how.
S0.feel: Calm and quietly pleased to have one less thing to think about.
S0.quote: Once it wrote that our strawberries were organic, and they're not, we spray them twice a season.
S0.fieldNote: He talks about the farm almost entirely through the shop and its customers. He uses AI in a careful, occasional way and learned to check it after one near-miss. His regular customer Mrs Hale is his picture of the people he serves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years gives everyone time to adjust, and that's sensible. Firms hiring fewer young people is a worry, mind. I'd say the schools and businesses need to work together on that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm fine with slow. But we take on two or three teenagers every summer in the shop and café, and that's their first job. If other places are hiring fewer beginners, I'll get forty applications for two places, and I'll have to say no to a lot of good kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to take on one extra teenager each summer, if the café's busy enough to pay for it, maybe five thousand over the season. I'd try a stock-ordering app for the shop once the farm shop down the road has used it a year. And I'd keep putting a bit by each month as usual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more for the young ones than for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you have to turn away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last year there was a lad, Owen, very shy, who wanted a café job and was useless at first and brilliant by August. In the slow picture, I'd have so many keen applicants that I'd never give an Owen a chance. That bothers me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your own kids do for a first job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the shop, which is the easy answer. Our eldest, Priya, is fourteen and already does the till on Sundays. But I don't want her stuck here just because nowhere else is hiring.

S1.say: Ten years gives everyone time to adjust, and that's sensible. Firms hiring fewer young people is a worry, and schools and businesses need to work on it together.
S1.think: Slow suits me, but the teenagers we take on every summer would struggle to find first jobs elsewhere. I'd get forty applications for two places and turn away a lot of good kids.
S1.do: Takes on one extra teenager each summer if the café can pay for it, about five thousand a season. Tries a stock-ordering app once a nearby farm shop has used it for a year, and keeps saving as usual.
S1.feel: Uneasy, mostly for the young people rather than his own family.
S1.quote: In the slow picture, I'd have so many keen applicants that I'd never give an Owen a chance.
S1.fieldNote: He immediately thought of the teenagers he hires, especially a shy boy who turned out brilliant. That story sums up his sense of fairness. His wait-and-see rule for technology is neat: copy the farm shop down the road after a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it needs careful handling, help for the people who lose out, but no panic. The politicians shouting doesn't help anybody. I'd say that to customers if they asked, but I'd keep it light, it's a shop, not a debate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this one worries me more than I'd let on. My customers are office workers from the estate. If they're facing layoffs and pay cuts, the first thing to go is the pricey Saturday brunch and the posh sausages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch the shop takings week by week, and if they dropped more than a tenth, I'd act. I'd bring in a cheaper range, a family meal box at about half the price of brunch, and push the eggs and potatoes, the basics. And I'd hold off on the second coffee machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's my customers who are in the firing line, and they're my income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you seen something like this before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When the big insurance office in town closed six years ago, we lost about a fifth of our weekend trade in three months. I remember standing in the empty café on a Saturday, thinking, where's everyone gone? It took two years to come back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Anjali say about the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say I'm being too gloomy, and then she'd make the meal boxes better than I'd planned. She's the shop's brains, honestly. I just carry the potatoes.

S2.say: It needs careful handling, with help for people who lose out but no panic. I'd keep it light with customers, because it's a shop, not a debate.
S2.think: This worries me more than I'd let on, because my customers are office workers. When they face layoffs, the pricey Saturday brunch and posh sausages go first.
S2.do: Watches the shop takings weekly and acts if they fall more than a tenth. Brings in a cheaper family meal box and pushes the basics, and holds off on the second coffee machine.
S2.feel: Anxious, because his customers are in the firing line and they are his income.
S2.quote: I remember standing in the empty café on a Saturday, thinking, where's everyone gone?
S2.fieldNote: There was a clear gap between his light public line and his private worry. He drew on a real memory of an office closure that cut his trade by a fifth. He credits his wife as the real brains of the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say both the companies and the government need to sit down and work out a fair share. No one side has all the answers. I'd try to keep the farm shop a place where people don't argue about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think this hits us hard, even though farming is safe. The estate empties of jobs, the weekend trade drops. The only upside is our land is worth more, but that's only on paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd turn the café toward cheaper, filling food, soup and bread, and maybe start a pay-what-you-can day once a month for people from the estate who've lost work. I'd ask the bank about fixing the mortgage. And I'd use the chat program to help write a plan for the shop, which I'd then get Anjali to rip apart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with a bit of sadness. It's watching your regulars struggle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A pay-what-you-can day costs you money. Why do it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because those people have kept us going for years, and you don't drop people when they're down. And honestly, when they're back on their feet, they'll remember who looked after them. It's kind and it's good business at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you sell any land, if prices boomed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Maybe a corner field for houses, if a developer offered silly money, but I'd want to talk to Mum first, it was Dad's field. I'd not decide that quickly.

S3.say: Both the companies and the government need to sit down and work out a fair share. No one side has all the answers, and the shop should be a place without arguments.
S3.think: This hits us hard even though farming is safe, because the estate empties of jobs and the weekend trade drops. Our land is worth more, but only on paper.
S3.do: Turns the café toward cheaper food like soup and bread and starts a monthly pay-what-you-can day. Asks the bank about fixing the mortgage and drafts a shop plan with a chat program for Anjali to rework.
S3.feel: Anxious, with a sadness at watching his regular customers struggle.
S3.quote: Those people have kept us going for years, and you don't drop people when they're down.
S3.fieldNote: He was one of the few farmers to see that the fast scenario hurts him despite farming being safe, because of who his customers are. His pay-what-you-can idea mixed kindness and business sense, and he said so openly. Selling land would be a family decision tied to his late father.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say go carefully, and make sure people aren't just thrown on the scrapheap. I'd also say farm shops like ours are the kind of place people will want more of, somewhere real. I'd put that on the shop's page, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a mix. Robots in the strawberry tunnels would solve the picking problem, which costs us a fortune every June. But robots in kitchens means the big café chains get cheaper, and my teenagers' jobs go too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lean hard into what robots can't do, the real people bit: pick-your-own strawberries, school visits, the piglets, Mum's scones. I'd rent a picking robot for the tunnels once the farm down the road had tried it. And I'd talk to Anjali about whether the café needs fewer staff, which would break my heart a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, but with some hope in it. Like we'd have to reinvent the shop, but we might manage it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you think people would want somewhere real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because after a week of talking to machines, people want a farmer with mud on his boots telling their kid about the pig. I've watched dads put their phones down to hold a lamb. That's the one thing we've got that no robot can fake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd rent a robot and cut café staff, but sell the human touch. Do those fit together?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not perfectly, no. I'd keep the people where customers can see them and put the robot where they can't, in the tunnels. Is that a bit sneaky? Maybe. It's also how I'd keep the place open.

S4.say: Go carefully and make sure people aren't thrown on the scrapheap. Farm shops like ours are the kind of real place people will want more of.
S4.think: Robots in the strawberry tunnels would solve our expensive June picking problem. But robots in kitchens make the big café chains cheaper and take my teenagers' jobs too.
S4.do: Leans into what robots can't do, such as pick-your-own, school visits and the piglets, and rents a picking robot once a neighbour has tried it. Talks with Anjali about whether the café needs fewer staff.
S4.feel: Alarmed but hopeful that the shop could be reinvented.
S4.quote: I've watched dads put their phones down to hold a lamb. That's the one thing we've got that no robot can fake.
S4.fieldNote: He found hope in selling the human touch, and the image of dads holding lambs was vivid. When I named the gap between renting a robot and selling humanity, he admitted it: people where customers see them, machines where they don't. That plan is pragmatic and slightly uncomfortable for him.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one with all the office jobs going, oddly, more than the robots. Our customers are office people, and if they go, the shop goes. What would help is support for people who lose their jobs, so they've still got a bit to spend, and maybe a business grant for small places like ours to get through a bad patch.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the places in between town and country. Nobody thinks of farm shops as part of the economy, but we're where the commuters meet the farmers. If they stop coming, we don't just lose money, we lose the link.

headlineQuote: I've watched dads put their phones down to hold a lamb. That's the one thing we've got that no robot can fake.
portrait: Colin is a 43-year-old who runs a mixed family farm with a farm shop and café at Elm Green, alongside his wife Anjali and his mother, who bakes on Saturdays. He sits in the political middle, uses AI now and then for shop posts, and waits for neighbours to prove new tools first. His worry rises not with the robots but with the office scenarios, because his customers are commuters from the new estate. He'd answer every scenario by leaning on people: hiring teenagers, a pay-what-you-can day, and the human touch robots can't fake.
biggestWorry: The fast scenario where office jobs go, because his customers are office workers and the shop depends on their weekend spending.
whatWouldHelp: Support for people who lose their jobs so they can still spend a little, and grants to help small businesses through a bad patch.
